lead: A digital audio or video file is usually two things at once: a container and the codecs inside it. The container is the box; the codec is the compressor. This separation lets one file format carry different codecs and lets a player choose the right decoder. It is why a .mp4 from a phone may play on a laptop, and why a .mkv may need a different player. This chapter explains the file formats and the numbers that describe their audio and video streams, with the compression algorithms left to later chapters.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for audio samples and video frames, and Chapter 4.4 for how a file format stores media and metadata.

sections.h3: A container is not a codec

blocks.text: A digital video file usually carries two compressed streams: one for pictures, one for sound. A codec (coder-decoder) compresses or decompresses one stream. A container, also called a wrapper format, packs those streams with timing information, an index and metadata into one file. A muxer writes the container. A player demuxes (separates) the streams and sends each to its decoder.

MP4 is a container. H.264 is a codec. The same .mp4 file can hold H.264 or H.265 video and AAC or MP3 audio. So the extension is a hint, not a promise. Audio-only formats include WAV, AIFF, MP3, AAC (.m4a), FLAC and Ogg Vorbis. Video containers include AVI, MP4, MOV, MKV and WebM.
A .mkv file can hold almost any codec; a .webm file is restricted to web codecs. The container decides what streams and metadata fit; the codec decides how small each stream becomes.

Audio is a sequence of samples. The sample rate f<sub>s</sub> is the number of samples per second, in hertz (Hz). CD audio uses 44,100 Hz. Bit depth b is the number of bits per sample; 16-bit is common. Channels C is 1 for mono and 2 for stereo. Uncompressed PCM audio stores every sample, so its bitrate is fixed:

blocks.where: R is the bitrate in bits per second (bit/s); f<sub>s</sub> is the sample rate in samples per second (Hz); b is the bit depth in bits per sample; C is the number of channels.

blocks.text: For CD audio: R = 44,100 × 16 × 2 = 1,411,200 bit/s = 1.4112 Mbps. WAV and AIFF often hold PCM. WAV is common on Windows; AIFF on Apple systems. MP3 is lossy and common at 128 kbps. AAC is a newer lossy audio codec, often inside MP4. FLAC is lossless: it reconstructs the exact PCM samples. Ogg Vorbis is lossy and usually sits in an Ogg container.

Bitrate can be constant (CBR) or variable (VBR). VBR spends more bits on difficult passages and fewer on silence. Sample rate is samples per second; bitrate is bits per second. They are different numbers.

sections.h3: Video: resolution, frame rate and containers

blocks.text: Video adds space and time. Resolution is width × height in pixels, such as 1920 × 1080. Frame rate is frames per second (fps). Full motion video is about 24 to 30 fps; cinema uses 24 fps, and many phone videos use 30 fps.

Compressed video bitrate is the number of bits per second for the video stream. A 1080p H.264 stream may use 4 to 8 Mbps; H.265 can reach similar quality at a lower bitrate. VBR changes the video bitrate with scene complexity; CBR holds it roughly fixed. Containers differ in the codecs they expect:

AVI is older and less flexible. MP4 is widely used for phones, cameras and the web. MOV is Apple's container. MKV is open and can hold many streams, subtitles and chapters. WebM targets the web with VP9 or AV1 video and Opus or Vorbis audio. H.264 (AVC) and H.265 (HEVC) are codecs, not containers.

figure.caption: A container such as MP4 holds video and audio streams that separate codecs have compressed. The muxer writes the streams and index into one file; the player demuxes and decodes them.

spec.title: Container and codecs
spec.aria: Two source streams, video and audio, pass through separate codecs into a muxer, then an MP4 file, then a player.

examples.question: An MP4 file holds H.264 video at 2 Mbps and AAC audio at 128 kbps. The video lasts 3 minutes. Find the file size, ignoring container overhead. Use 1 MB = 10^6 bytes.
examples.answer: The file size is 47.88 MB, ignoring container overhead.
examples.check:
video_bps = 2_000_000
audio_bps = 128_000
duration_s = 3 * 60
video_MB = video_bps * duration_s / 8 / 1_000_000
audio_MB = audio_bps * duration_s / 8 / 1_000_000
total_MB = video_MB + audio_MB
print(video_MB)
print(audio_MB)
print(total_MB)

traps: MP4 is a container, not a codec. H.264 or H.265 is the codec inside.
A .mp3 file is audio only; it cannot carry a video stream.
Do not confuse bitrate (bits per second) with sample rate (samples per second).
The file extension does not guarantee the codec; a .mp4 may hold H.264 or H.265, and a .mkv may hold many codecs.
Full motion video is about 24 to 30 frames per second, not 24 to 30 frames in total.

quiz.q: What is a container in a media file?
quiz.a: A container, or wrapper format, packs compressed streams, timing, an index and metadata into one file. MP4 and MKV are containers.

quiz.q: Why can two .mp4 files use different codecs?
quiz.a: MP4 is only the container. It can carry video such as H.264 or H.265 and audio such as AAC or MP3. The codec is chosen when the file is made.

quiz.q: Find the PCM bitrate for 48 kHz sampling, 16-bit depth and stereo. Give the answer in bit/s and Mbps.
A 2-minute MP4 has video at 1.5 Mbps and audio at 96 kbps. Find its size, ignoring overhead. Use 1 MB = 10^6 bytes.
Name two audio-only formats and two video containers.
quiz.a: Audio-only: WAV, MP3, FLAC or Ogg Vorbis. Video containers: MP4, AVI, MOV, MKV or WebM.

quiz.q: Explain CBR and VBR in one or two sentences.
quiz.a: CBR keeps the bitrate roughly constant. VBR changes the bitrate with the complexity of the content, spending more bits on difficult parts and fewer on simple parts.

quiz.q: Why is MP4 called a wrapper format?
quiz.a: It wraps separate video and audio streams, plus timing, an index and metadata, into one file. It does not itself define the compression; codecs such as H.264 and AAC do that.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer video codecs such as AV1 aim for better compression without licence fees. Container features such as fragmented MP4 matter for streaming, which Unit 6 covers. Media metadata standards can describe access rights and content details outside the basic container. Search for AV1, fragmented MP4 and media container metadata if you meet them in a project.
